UAH Archives separately catalogs an item titled ‘1835 Union Chapel Church, Hazel Green, 1972’ in the Harvie P. Jones papers, Box 73, Folder 9; the catalog page does not identify a denomination or African American congregation.

Source: Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands Claim Division; FamilySearch images 429 and 430 of 1107; NARA image group 007636377
Evidence: On April 2, 1870, Huntsville agent John H. Wager requested information for Monroe Threatt, late private, Company C, 16th U.S.C.T. Threatt stated that he gave his discharge to Mr. Baker of Courtland, Alabama, in early 1867, believed he had been mustered out in 1866, received no receipt for the discharge, and wanted to know the condition of his bounty claim. His post-office address was Jones X Roads, Limestone County. The Claim Division reported that its records did not show receipt of the certificate, referred the inquiry to the Second Auditor, and returned it to Huntsville with an endorsement.
Why It Is Important: The paired documents directly identify a Black Union veteran living at Jones Cross Roads and explain how a private intermediary’s possession of his discharge could produce a missing federal claim certificate. They provide a named person, precise place, unit, intermediary, and administrative trail for mapping the wider Jones-area community and studying archival loss.
Connections: Jones Cross Roads; Limestone County; Courtland; Huntsville Freedmen’s Bureau; Company C, 16th U.S.C.T.; Mr. Baker; missing discharge and bounty certificate. The place name may be relevant to Jones landholding or Black community networks near Madison County, but it does not establish ownership, kinship, or an Avalon connection.
Conclusions: Monroe Threatt is a strong geographic and community-network lead, not a Jones-lineage identification. The paired records support a specific mechanism for archival erasure: a claimant surrendered his original discharge to an intermediary without a receipt, while the federal office later lacked the certificate.
Questions: Where exactly was Jones Cross Roads in 1870, and whose land or road junction supplied the name? Who lived nearby in the 1870 census, tax records, deeds, church records, and voter lists? Did Monroe Threatt have Jones neighbors, relatives, witnesses, or former enslavers? Who was Mr. Baker of Courtland, and do his claim files or business records survive?

Document Title: From a Kingdom in Wales to a Cotton Farm in Alabama
Source: Huntsville History Collection
Evidence: The article proposes a multigenerational route from alleged descent from Llywelyn ap Gruffudd to Rev. Rowland Jones (born 1608, Swinbrook, Oxfordshire), then Rowland Jones Jr. migrating from Little Kimble, Buckinghamshire, to Virginia about 1674 and serving Bruton Parish at Williamsburg. It next links Orlando Jones descendants to Martha Washington and Captain John Jones, places Captain John and his son Llewellen at Valley Forge in 1778, and states that Llewellen later migrated to North Alabama with the Georgia Faction. In Alabama it says he purchased 640 acres at the 1809 land sale, owned more than 1,000 acres by 1811, acquired property through an Irby Jones debt, named Avalon, purchased Druid’s Grove and Seclusion, and transmitted properties through his children. It further states that Alexander inherited Avalon, fathered children with an enslaved woman, and that descendants remained until the college-campus appropriation. Nearly all of these lineage and migration claims are uncited on the page.
Why It Is Important: Central secondary evidence for the published Wales/England-to-Virginia-to-Alabama migration tradition and the proposed kinship-plantation network. It directly preserves claims about debt-based land acquisition, plantation inheritance, Black descendants, and later UAH land appropriation. Lack of citations affects claim confidence but does not negate the article as evidence of the narrative itself.
Connections: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd; Rev. Rowland Jones; Rowland Jones Jr.; Orlando Jones; Captain John Jones; Llewellen Jones; Irby Jones; Alexander P. Jones; Martha Washington; Bruton Parish; Williamsburg; Valley Forge; Georgia Faction; 1809 Huntsville land sale; Avalon; Druid’s Grove; Seclusion; Jones descendants; UAH campus.
Conclusions: The article is evidence that a coherent migration, inheritance, and Black-descendant narrative was publicly articulated and circulated. It is not by itself conclusive proof of each pedigree or property claim. Its evidentiary value therefore operates at two levels: high for the existence and content of the public narrative, and variable for the historical events asserted within it.
Questions: Identify the author and research files; locate parish registers for Rowland Jones, Virginia wills and deeds, Revolutionary service and Valley Forge evidence, the 1776 commission, Georgia Faction migration records, 1809 federal land-sale entries, Irby Jones debt/chancery documentation, deeds for Avalon/Druid’s Grove/Seclusion, Alexander P. Jones probate and slave records, and UAH acquisition files. Determine the source for the unnamed enslaved woman and descendants. Which of the three same-named Llewellen Jones men who settled in north Alabama is the actual Avalon founder, and can I find a primary source (deed, will, court record) that distinguishes him from the other two before treating any single VA-origin record as confirmed?

Document Title: Turrentine, Administrator, v. Perkins et al.
Document Type: Primary legal source — Alabama Supreme Court case transcription
Source: Alabama Department of Archives and History, Alabama Supreme Court Case Files
Evidence: The case states that Alexander S. Perkins died intestate on or about January 23, 1867, and that letters of administration were granted March 8, 1867. It identifies his widow, Elizabeth or Bettie H. Perkins, and children Alexander S. and Maria E.; describes Madison and Limestone County lands; and discusses bonds or notes jointly executed by Alexander P. Jones and Perkins in 1861–1862. The creditor schedules also list “Sigh Jones (Cold) 882.18,” elsewhere rendered “Cy Jones (Col).” A filing register specifies: “June 24th Sigh Jones, (Col), 1 account, due Jan 1st 1863, $882.18 — This claim taken out by consent.” Bettie F. Perkins later objected that the claim was not filed according to law, that the estate was not indebted to him, that it was barred by limitations, and that it lacked verification.
Why It Is Important: This is authoritative evidence for Perkins’s death and estate chronology, corrects narratives that place his death two years after inheriting Avalon, and documents a financial relationship between Perkins and Alexander P. Jones. The Cy/Sigh Jones material is especially important because it records a Black claimant asserting a large account dating to slavery and shows the procedural and substantive objections used against the claim. The record does not disclose what labor, goods, property, or transaction created the debt.
Connections: Alexander Spotswood Perkins; Elizabeth/Bettie H. Perkins; Alexander S. Perkins; Maria E. Perkins; Alexander P. Jones; Cy/Sigh Jones, identified as colored; Madison and Limestone County lands; debt, bonds, estate administration, creditor claims, and later chancery proceedings. The spelling Cy/Sigh is unresolved but appears to refer to the same claimant.
Conclusions: Strongly supports a death date on or about January 23, 1867, rather than 1869 or 1877, and a documented financial relationship between Perkins and Alexander P. Jones. It also proves that a Black claimant named Cy/Sigh Jones filed an $882.18 account due January 1, 1863 and that Bettie Perkins contested it. It does not prove the claim’s underlying basis, that Cy/Sigh was enslaved by Perkins or APJ, that the claim was fraudulent, or that it was ultimately allowed or paid.
Questions: Which parcels in the pleadings overlap Avalon or other Jones-Perkins properties? What happened between the January death and March administration? What created Cy/Sigh Jones’s $882.18 account in 1863: wages, skilled labor, goods, a loan, hired-out labor, or another transaction? Was he enslaved, free, or hired by Perkins or APJ? Can probate vouchers, account books, testimony, tax records, or later court orders establish whether the claim was verified, allowed, rejected, settled, or paid?
Citation: Turrentine, Administrator, v. Perkins et al., Alabama Supreme Court Case Files, Alabama Department of Archives and History, transcription, https://archives.alabama.gov/research/docs/collections/supreme-court/SC00287_Turrentine_v_Perkins_transcription.pdf (accessed July 24, 2026).
H2 Legal, educational, archival & histor: Supports: court chronology corrects later narratives; procedural treatment of Cy/Sigh Jones’s claim illuminates archival and legal barriers
H3 Black Jones lineage & genealogical co: Unresolved Black Jones claimant: Cy/Sigh Jones; no lineage established
H6 Plantation kinship, land & economy: Supports: land, debt, and Jones-Perkins economic relationships
H7 Black agency, Reconstruction & instit: Supports: Black claimant asserted a substantial account dating to 1863
Thesis Category: Institutional Erasure / Plantation Economy / Black Claims
Notes: Do not describe the claim as wages or as erased without finding its basis and final disposition. Preserve both Cy and Sigh as spelling variants.

Source: The University of Alabama in Huntsville

They support investigation of institutional handling of Avalon but do not prove cancellation, motive, or responsibility. The 2021 newsletter closes the earlier completion-status gap: a completed marker existed and had been delivered to UAH, although installation and dedication remain unverified. The 2026 source documents continued fieldwork and specific search locations.
Connections: UAH Archives and Special Collections; Department of History; Avalon; Union Grove Gallery; Morton Hall; University Drive; Jones-Perkins Cemetery; archaeology; GPR; public memory and memorialization.
Conclusions: Supported: UAH announced memorialization in 2019; a completed Avalon/Jones-Perkins marker had arrived and was being kept at UAH by spring 2021; archaeology continued through 2026. Unresolved: whether the marker was installed or dedicated and what the 2026 dig found.
Questions: Was the fall unveiling held? Were donations received or spent? Do Foundation, Archives, History Department, facilities, planning, advancement, or administrative records contain proposals, minutes, contracts, emails, donor files, or cancellation decisions? Who approved or changed the project, and when? How should the absence of a public completion or cancellation notice be interpreted without overstating it? Where is the completed marker now, was it installed or dedicated, and what records document custody and decisions after spring 2021? What field notes, maps, artifact catalogs, photographs, and reports resulted from the 2026 dig?

Source: Lewellen Jones; Madison County probate loose Case No. 223, images 332-338; inventory cross-reference to Probate Record Book 2, page 153
Evidence: Lewellen Jones’s loose probate Case No. 223 records an estate count of ‘Slaves 47.’ His will appointed his eldest son John N. S. Jones and Gross Scruggs Sr., both of Madison County, Alabama Territory, as executors. A January 1832 settlement identifies Gross Scruggs as one of the executors settling the estate, demonstrating administration lasting roughly twelve years after Lewellen’s death. The will states that Frances A. M. Perkins had already received valuable property in enslaved people in Virginia and divides the remaining enslaved property between John N. S. Jones and Alexander P. Jones. The case index points to the Inventory of Estate in Probate Record Book 2, page 153.
Why It Is Important: The records establish a sustained Jones–Scruggs fiduciary and planter-capital relationship rather than a merely incidental signature. Scruggs participated in administering an estate containing 47 enslaved people, land, debts, and inheritance transfers across the Jones and Perkins branches.
Connections: Lewellen Jones; John N. S. Jones; Alexander P. Jones; Frances A. M. Perkins; Gross Scruggs Sr.; Madison County; Virginia; Lawrence County; Jones-Perkins-Scruggs plantation and estate network
Conclusions: Verified: Gross Scruggs Sr. was co-executor and remained involved in settlement through 1832. Verified: the estate cover recorded ‘Slaves 47.’ Not proven: that Scruggs personally received, purchased, hired, or transferred any of the 47 people, or that Jones estate capital passed to a later Huntsville institution.
Questions: Obtain Probate Record Book 2, page 153 and all continuation pages, vouchers, executor accounts, hire records, receipts, and distributions. Test whether Scruggs handled particular named people, land, debts, or payments and whether any later Scruggs property or capital entered institutional ownership.

Notes: Original loose-case cover reviewed July 31, 2026 and confirms the handwritten aggregate ‘Slaves 47.’ No individual identities should be generated from that count. The separate bound inventory is explicitly cross-referenced at Probate Record Book 2, page 153. The will execution year remains unresolved between 1815 and 1818. [2026-08-04] I found a verbatim transcription of this same 1818 will of Lewellen (Llewellen) Jones at the Alabama Department of Archives and History, in a Valley Leaves Vol 44 Issue 3 (March 2010) article, hgpub item 32734 (https://digital.archives.alabama.gov/digital/collection/hgpub/id/32734). It names daughter Frances A.M. Perkins and sons John N.S. Jones and Alexander P. Jones as heirs/executors, which corroborates what I already had from the Ancestry probate images. [2026-08-04 SAME-DAY UPDATE] I now have the full verbatim will text, transcribed from Madison County Probate Record 2, p. 106: "Will of Lewellen Jones -- In the name of God amen, I Lewellen Jones of Madison County, Madison County, Alabama Territory being of sound mind, do make this my last will and testament ... to my beloved daughter Frances A. M. Perkins, I give and bequeath that tract of land lying on Spring Creek in Lawrence County, Alabama Territory, containing seven hundred and thirty four acres and twenty hundredths acres ... furthermore, to my beloved daughter Frances A. M. Perkins I give and bequeath the sum of three thousand seven hundred and seventy seven dollars fifty cents to her and her heirs forever, and no more, having given her other valuable property in Negroes previous to this in the state of Virginia. After all my just debts are paid, I give and bequeath unto my two well beloved sons, John N. S. Jones and Alexander P. Jones ... all the remainder of my estate ... deducting two thousand dollars from the portion of my eldest son John N. S. Jones ... Lastly I do appoint my eldest son John N. S. Jones and ? Scruggs ? both of Madison County, Alabama Territory, executors ... this 20th day of October 1818. Signed and acknowledged in the presence of Benjamin W. Burford, William A. Powell, Henry Moore." This resolves the 1815-vs-1818 execution-date question in favor of October 20, 1818. The reference to Frances having already received enslaved people 'in the state of Virginia' is a new, important detail -- it documents Virginia-to-Alabama transport of enslaved people by this family predating the will itself. See also DB1 row 218 (two letters to J.N.S. Jones, same estate) and DB3 row 68 (source article, same estate).

Document Title: Will and biographical record of Rev. Rowland Jones (1644-1688), first minister of Bruton Parish -- land distribution to sons Robert, William, Orlando
Document Type: Abstracted will and historical article (secondary source citing York County court and parish records)

Evidence: Rowland Jones (b. 1644 Swinbrook, Oxfordshire, son of the elder Rev. Rowland Jones, vicar of Wendover, Bucks., who willed Sept. 1, 1665) matriculated Merton College, Oxford, Nov. 13, 1663, and became first minister of Bruton Parish, Middle Plantation (later Williamsburg), Virginia, serving 1674 until his death April 23, 1688. His will, dated Aug. 15, 1687 and proved Dec. 13, 1688, distributed: the home plantation to wife Ann Jones for life, then to son Orlando; a 400-acre Pomunkey Neck plantation to son Robert (then William, then Orlando, then daughter Anna Maria); 200 acres on Chickahominy Branches (bought from David Newell, Charles City Co.) to son William; and a 40-acre "mill swamp and pond" to sister Jane Gooch for life. He is buried behind the chancel rail of Bruton Parish Church; his Latin tombstone epitaph names him "Pastor Primus & delectissimus" of Bruton after 14 years' service.
Why It Is Important: This is the earliest documented land-holding generation in the direct Avalon lineage -- establishes that the Jones family's pattern of dividing named home-plantations among sons (mirrored two generations later when Lewellen Jones divided "Avalon" and "Druid's Grove" between his own two sons, per row 307) already existed in 17th-century Virginia. Names Pomunkey Neck and Chickahominy Branches as the family's earliest known Virginia landholdings, predating the family's move to Bedford Co. and then to Madison/Limestone Cos., Alabama.

Document Title: John Nelson Spotswood Jones's Law Office as the Site of Huntsville's First Public Library (1818-1819) -- corroborated by two independent sources
Document Type: Secondary source (local history), corroborated across two independent publications
Source: (1) Paul A. Hays, From Carnegie to Fort Book: The History of the Huntsville-Madison County Public Library; (2) Huntsville Historical Review, Vol. 44, No. 2 (Fall/Winter 2019), Huntsville-Madison County Historical Society
Evidence: In July 1818 Dr. Thomas Fearn wrote to Clement Clay urging the creation of a subscription library in Huntsville, then still Alabama Territory; a meeting followed and roughly $2,000-3,000 was subscribed. The Huntsville Library Company issued shares (e.g., Share No. 59 to William Atwood, $20, dated 10 Dec. 1818, signed Robert Fearn, Treasurer, and Thomas G. Percy, President). The library was for men-subscribers only. Books were first assumed to be housed in Mr. Minor's office in the courthouse, but 'the law office of John Nelson Spotswood Jones is credited with the location of the first library in October 1819, as Jones opened his law office in September 1819.' A newspaper notice of the era states: 'the Books are opened at the office of J. N. S. Jones, Esq. next door to the Printing Office on the street leading to Ditto's Landing [current Madison & Whitesburg],' open Tuesdays and Fridays 11:30 AM-12:30 PM, John Boardman, Librarian. The HHR Vol. 44 No. 2 article independently confirms: 'The library, for gentlemen only, was located in the Madison Street law office of John Nelson Spotswood Jones and opened on Tuesdays and Thursdays while Jones was out to lunch,' and notes it was the first public library in the Alabama Territory. A replica of the Jones law office stands today in Constitution Village, Huntsville, facing Madison Street next to the Boardman printing building.
Why It Is Important: This is a significant, independently-corroborated civic-history fact directly tying a founding-era Jones-family member (already tracked in this database in connection with the Madison County Jones/Perkins civic elite, cf. DB1 row 451) to a specific, still-commemorated physical site and civic institution in Huntsville -- the first public library in the entire Alabama Territory. It is directly relevant to the project's 'institutional knowledge/public memory' research angle: the library was subscription-only (for paying gentlemen), illustrating how Huntsville's earliest civic and cultural institutions were built by and for a small propertied white elite in a county whose wealth depended on enslaved labor.
Connections: John Nelson Spotswood Jones (Madison County founding-era Jones/Perkins elite, DB1 row 451); Dr. Thomas Fearn; Clement Clay; Robert Fearn; Thomas G. Percy; John Boardman; Constitution Village, Huntsville.
Conclusions: Two independent secondary sources corroborate the same underlying fact (Jones's law office as the first library site, Sept./Oct. 1819), which strengthens confidence in the fact itself, though both ultimately likely draw on the same underlying 1818-1819 newspaper notices as their primary source.
Questions: Can the original 1818-1819 Huntsville newspaper notices (quoted in both secondary sources) be located and viewed directly as primary sources? Is there a surviving deed or lease record for the law office site itself, and does it name the specific street/lot in a way that can be mapped onto later Madison County property records tied to the Jones family? Does the Constitution Village replica's own historical marker or exhibit text cite additional primary sources not captured here?

Document Title: Reuben Parker Jones, Madison County: 1830 census (0 enslaved) → 1840 census (14 enslaved) — a decade of wealth accumulation

This is the largest single list of enslaved names in the Jones records so far, and every name goes on the record as written. Source: Ancestry.com, "Jones Family (Avalon Plantation)" family tree, tree ID 210795668 (unsourced lead); Freedman's Bank Signature Book, Huntsville, Alabama branch, Roll 01, image ALM816_1-0015, application no. 29, Columbus Jones, October 2, 1867 (downloaded and preserved to the Avalon project archive)
Evidence: An entry in the "Jones Family (Avalon Plantation)" tree for a woman recorded as "Elizabeth (Enslaved)" (b. c.1781, Talladega County, Alabama; d. fall of 1861) lists two successive unions — with Llewellen Jones, then with Turner Moore — producing several Jones-surnamed children: Columbus, Reuben, Turner Jr., Wade, Isabella (later Scruggs), Queen Ann, and a daughter also named Elizabeth. The tree's "Talladega County" birthplace is anachronistic: the county was not created until December 18, 1832, from the Creek cession (Ala. Acts 1832, ann. sess., no. 11, sec. 2) — a data-quality flag on the profile itself. The tree entry is an unsourced index, not proof, and is treated strictly as a lead. It gains partial, independent corroboration from a primary source: the Freedman's Bank Signature Book record for Columbus Jones (Huntsville, application no. 29, October 2, 1867), in which Columbus names brothers Reuben and Turner who died at the same place as their unnamed mother, herself recorded as having died in the fall of ’61 (the tree gives fall of 1861) The matching sibling names (Reuben, Turner) and shared death location are consistent with, but do not confirm, the tree's claim that all three shared the same mother. The mother's name is not stated in the Freedman's Bank record itself; "Elizabeth" is supplied only by the tree. This finding does not resolve whether this Elizabeth is the same woman named in the 1820 manumission act, and it is not treated as settling that question.
Why It Is Important: A concrete, testable lead on the maternity of Columbus and Reuben Jones — the project's central unresolved kinship question — with a built-in verification path (1861 records) and a built-in caution (the anachronistic birthplace).
Connections: DB1 row 255 (Turner Moore & Elizabeth Enslaved couple, merged/duplicated spouse groupings); DB1 row 538 (Freedman's Bank corrected reading: mother Eliza, brothers Reuben and Turner); DB1 row 179 (the 1820 manumission act); DB1 row 177 (Llewellen Jones second family); DB2 "Enslaved People Research Leads" rows 143-144 and 147-153; Hoksbergen & DeNeefe (July 2026) on the age problem
Conclusions: Unresolved/Lead — the two-union sequence, the seven-children list, and the identification of this Elizabeth with the 1820 manumission woman are all unproven. The Freedman's Bank corroboration covers sibling names and death timing only, not the mother's name.
Questions: Locate an 1861 Madison County, Alabama probate, estate, or death record for an enslaved woman in the Jones/Moore household; independently re-review the Freedman's Bank record image for any additional legible detail in its remarks column.

Document Title: Read-only review of the "Jones Family (Avalon Plantation)" Ancestry tree (tree ID 210795668): duplications, conflicts, and data-quality assessment (September 20, 2026) — from note [131], section 20
Document Type: Research report — read-only review of an unsourced genealogical index (a lead/conflict log, not findings)
Source: Ancestry.com, "Jones Family (Avalon Plantation)" member tree, tree ID 210795668, on the author's UAH Ancestry account; reviewed in strictly read-only mode on September 20, 2026 — nothing was added, edited, merged, accepted, or rejected. See note [120].
Evidence: The tree is an unsourced index, and every item below is a lead or a conflict, not a finding. The tree contains two records for the same patriarch — "Turner Moore Jones Sr" and "Turner Moore" (both b. 1780, d. March 1867) — and two records for his wife — "Eliza Elizabeth Jones" and "Elizabeth Enslaved" (both b. c.1781, d. 1861). Because of this duplication, Columbus Jones appears as Turner's son in one record and as his grandson in the other. The "Turner Moore" record carries an unsourced 1792 marriage in Louisa, Virginia — the tree's only Virginia-roots link — and its pedigree chain is chronologically incoherent (Alexander P. Jones appears both as Turner's son and in his ancestor chain). Conflict: Columbus's attached Freedman's Bank record (application no. 29, October 2, 1867, Huntsville) names his wife as Henrietta, while the 1860 census entry and the tree show a wife named Adeline; the conflict is unresolved. The tree's member profiles identify Shandy Wesley Jones (1816–1886) as Reuben Jones's half-brother through Eliza's first marriage to Capt. Llewellen Jones, but the tree's own placement of Shandy is inconsistent with that relationship. No Southern Claims Commission records are attached to any person in the tree; one unreviewed hint — "U.S., Southern Claims Commission, Disallowed and Barred Claims, 1871–1880," Shandy Jones, Huntsville, court date January 1, 1873 — names participants Calvin Jones and Willis Jones, who do not appear in the tree; the indexed hint does not display claim numbers, so claims 18,680 and 9,105 remain unverified from this source (cf. DB1 rows 626 and 220, which carry the claim numbers independently). The Perkins line is a dead end in the tree: "Frances A. M. Jones Perkins" has no mother, no spouse, and no attached records despite the Perkins surname. Nearly every birth, death, and marriage fact in the tree is unsourced; only residence facts carry records.
Why It Is Important: A controlled, read-only data-quality baseline for the member tree this project keeps drawing leads from — it documents exactly where the tree contradicts itself, so no one cites it as authority for the relationships it asserts.
Connections: DB1 rows 177, 255 (tree-based Elizabeth material); DB1 row 538 (Freedman's Bank corrected reading); DB1 row 626 (Shandy SCC No. 18,680, affidavit Jan 1, 1873, witnesses Calvin & Willis Jones); DB1 row 220 (Shandy Limestone claim No. 9,105); DB1 row 179 (1820 manumission act); note [120] (the review's own citation note)
Conclusions: Assessment, not evidence: the tree is an unsourced index usable for leads only. Its internal contradictions (duplicated Turner/Eliza profiles; Columbus as both son and grandson; APJ in two generations; Henrietta vs. Adeline; Shandy's inconsistent placement; the Perkins dead end) are documented here so they are not mistaken for findings.
Questions: Resolve the Henrietta/Adeline conflict (Columbus's wife); check Shandy's placement against records; pull the SCC case files behind the Jan 1, 1873 hint; trace Frances A. M. Jones Perkins's parentage beyond the tree.

Document Title: Same-name cautions: the 1868 Emma Jones on the McCalley plantation census; Mahala Lowe, sister of Reuben Lowe; and the (Phil)ip Woodson planter
Source: WikiTree, 'Thomas McCalley Plantation, Madison County, Alabama' — https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Space:Thomas_McCalley_Plantation,_Madison_County,_Alabama (cites FamilySearch image 3QS7-99LD-YHGF, M1900 roll 19, image 12 of 82, 1868 census p. 20). Gillain (huntsville7, Dec. 13, 1869).
Evidence: An 1868 Madison County Freedmen's Census, as transcribed on the WikiTree McCalley plantation page, lists Rosa Jones, 40, house servant, with children Frances 18, Leroy 14, Sarah 6, Emma 3 — associated with Thomas McCalley's plantation. Reuben Lowe's 1869 bank entry names his sisters Ellen, Sarah, and Mahala, all living with him on 'Jones on ?Miarh River' (DB1 rows 642/645 lead). A (Phil)ip Woodson appears in the bank books as plantation/employer near Huntsville 1867–1870: Thomas Scruggs, 'Plantation: Phil Woodson'; James Withers, 'Plantation: Philip Woodson near Huntsville.' John Henry Russell Davis notes his brother William Gauch 'resides with Mr. Woodson on the mountain.' Benj. Gillain names 'Lisey Woodson' as a sister.
Why It Is Important: Three traps fenced before they can do damage: (1) the 1868 Emma is three years old and tied to a different census — she cannot be imported as the 1865 Emma Jones without image-verified continuity; (2) a Mahala Lowe existed in Madison County at the same time as Mahela Jones — same first name, different family, do not merge; (3) the Woodson surname in 1860s Madison County belonged to a white planter too, so the name alone proves nothing about enslavement.
Connections: DB1 rows 735–737; DB4 row 242; paper [195]; bibliography Section AD
Conclusions: Unresolved across the board: no verified 1870 census match for the four-name cluster; the McCalley Emma and Mahala Lowe stay fenced as same-name cautions; the Woodson planter is context for the surname. Thomas McCalley is not a confirmed enslaver connection — no McCalley FAN investigation opened.
Questions: Does the 1868 census image (M1900 roll 19, image 12) show the Rosa Jones household as transcribed? Is Mahala Lowe traceable after 1869? Who was (Phil)ip Woodson — and did any Black Jones ever name him as enslaver? (Woodson Jones's bank entry names no master.)

Document Title: Do-not-merge fence: Tuscaloosa Adeline Jones (wife of Reuben Jones, free Black blacksmith, 1854–1860) vs. Madison County Adaline/Adeline Jones (1865 census index; 1867 Woodson Jones bank remarks)
Source: Hoksbergen & DeNeefe, 'Keeping Up with the Joneses: Tracing the Lives and Legacies of Two Reconstruction-Era Legislators from Madison County,' Alabama Review vol. 79, no. 3 (July 2026) — Tuscaloosa Adeline documented 1854–1860; plus this morning's Bureau-cluster finds (DB1 rows 735–738: 1865 Madison County index of Adaline Jones; Woodson Jones bank remarks 'Adeline resides in Huntsville, Ala.').
Evidence: Tuscaloosa: Adeline Jones, wife of free Black blacksmith Reuben Jones, documented in Tuscaloosa 1854–1860 (per the Hoksbergen/DeNeefe article in my Drive, local copy research_notes/shandy-identity-20260920/). Madison County: Adaline Jones indexed as one of four consecutive 1865 Madison County Black Jones entries (NMAAHC fbs-1662423774659-1662425318805-0, M1900 roll 19); and 'Adeline resides in Huntsville, Ala.' in Woodson Jones's Dec. 24, 1867 Freedman's Bank remarks. Different county, different documented household, different evidentiary base.
Why It Is Important: The Adeline name appears in two counties with two completely different life stories. Writing them into one woman would manufacture a migration and a marriage that no record supports — so the fence stays up.
Connections: DB1 rows 735–738 (Madison cluster); DB4 row 242; paper [195]; bibliography Sections AD (and the Hoksbergen/DeNeefe article's own bibliography entry); shandy-identity-20260920 notes

Tuscaloosa Adeline (Tuscaloosa County, 1854–1860, household of Reuben Jones) and Madison Adaline/Adeline (Madison County, 1865 index + 1867 bank remarks, possibly mother/sister context of Woodson Jones) are recorded as two separate people. Document Title: 1835-007 — Administrator of Armstead Minor v. Executor of Thomas V. Jones: Margana, Jim, Mary — full firsthand read

Evidence: Three enslaved people named, all in the deed of trust of June 14, 1832 (Armstead Minor → trustee William L. Goggin, securing a $180.30 bond debt to Thomas V. Jones; acknowledged by all three parties before Robt. Mitchell, Clerk): Margana (“a woman,” ~16–17), Jim (“a boy”), Mary (“a girl”) — plus “their future increase.” Margana was the only one sold: at the trustee sale on November 24, 1832 at the courthouse door in Liberty, Thomas V. Evidence: In 1821 Peter Blow executed a deed of trust to John N. S. Jones securing a $2,000 note with the NW 1/4 of Section 29, Township 3 North, Range 1 West (Basis Meridian) — the land on which Oakwood College now stands — "and the following slaves to wit, a negro man Luke about twenty two years of age a man named Will about twenty one years of age a man named Sam about twenty years of age a boy named Dred a boy about sixteen years of age a boy named Isaac about thirteen years of age a Girl named Phillis about seventeen years of age, a woman named Hannah about forty five years of age & Solomon a man about sixty years of age" (Madison Co. Deed Book G, pp. 163–165). A second 1821 deed of trust covered the same land and people (Beverly Hughes, trustee, for John Key of Virginia, Blow's son-in-law; Deed Book G, pp. 328–330). On Dec 7, 1821 Blow sold the parcel — received by U.S. grant Oct 5, 1819 — to James W. Camp for $5,000 (Deed Book H, pp. 79–80). The article argues the Madison deeds show Sam and Dred were distinct people (Sam b. ~1801; Dred b. ~1805) and that Sam/Dred Scott likely took the name Dred from a deceased younger brother; no trace of Dred, Isaac, or Phillis after 1821. Mary Ann Blow married John Key Dec 8, 1819 (d. Aug 7, 1826). June 1989 Editor's Leaf follow-up: Blow moved to Lauderdale County after the 1821 sale (witness to a will by Aug 11, 1822; chancery complaint 1823, decree 1827); Joshua Willis v. Document Title: ALM816 frame 673 (Mobile): Jones names on the frame and the S. W. Jones verdict [assessment]
Source: Registers of Signatures of Depositors in Branches of the Freedman's Savings and Trust Company, 1865-1874, National Archives Microfilm Publication M816, Record Group 101, National Archives and Records Administration, roll 2 (Mobile, Alabama branch), frame 673 (Research-Leads_Unidentified-Archival-Image-ALM816_undated_[ALM816_2-0673.jpg].pdf); frame-level assessment
Evidence: Jones names on the frame: depositors — 'Chas. W. Jones' (7961) is the only Jones depositor. Family fields — 7961 names father S. W. Jones, mother C. Wiley Jones, one sibling S. C. Jones. Other entries naming Jones: none — entries 7958 (Rowan), 7959 (Hale), and 7960 (Burch) name no Jones in any parent, sibling, or spouse field. The four remaining entries on the frame (7953 Davis, 7955 Taylor, 7956 Bunchum?, 7957 Jas. A. Thomas Lewis) were not deep-read (out of scope); no Jones names were observed in the overview pass. Verdict: Charles W. Jones is a Black Tuscaloosa-born man, age 22 (b. ~1851), literate (signed his name), living in Mobile by 1873. His stated father 'S. W. Jones' is a plausible-but-unproven match to Shandy Wesley Jones (b. 1816 per Hoksbergen & DeNeefe 2026): the initials fit, the generation fits (Shandy ~35 at Charles's birth), Shandy was in Tuscaloosa by 1837, and the Freedman's Bank served the free Black community Shandy belonged to. Against merging: (1) 'S. W.' is initials only — could be Samuel, Solomon, etc.; (2) mother 'C. Wiley Jones' and sibling 'S. C. Jones' are unattested in current Shandy scholarship (his documented mother is Elizabeth, manumitted 1820); (3) Charles's move to Mobile is a new, unverified migration; (4) no direct evidence links S. W. Jones to Shandy Wesley Jones. Charles W. Jones stays DISTINCT — this is a lead, not an identification. The Mobile-branch context matters: this is NOT a Tuscaloosa record — Charles had left Tuscaloosa by 1873.
Why It Is Important: The fence is the finding — a tempting Shandy match is held apart on initials alone, which is exactly the discipline the rest of the Jones identity work depends on.
Connections: FAN: two new network names — 'C. Wiley Jones' ('Wiley' possibly her maiden name) and 'S. C. Jones.' Search them in the census and DB2; do not merge with any existing row without direct evidence. DB2-staged: Charles W. Jones; S. W. Jones; C. Wiley Jones; S. C. Jones — all fenced from existing rows (see DB4 rows 548–549). DB1 rows 1331–1335. Paper notes [374]–[375].
Conclusions: Lead — held distinct. The right next steps are census verification (1870: Charles W. Jones ~19 in Tuscaloosa or Mobile; S. W. Jones households in Tuscaloosa 1870), the M817 deposit-ledger index for account 7961, and a full Mobile-branch M816 sweep for other Jones accounts (father, mother, sibling may hold their own accounts).
Questions: Whether any Mobile Jones account names a former enslaver or plantation — check the sweep for that field.

Document Title: 1816-022 Henry Trucks v William R. Jones: rent-and-corn arbitration (1811–1814) — William R. Jones appears only as a Bedford creditor/landlord; NO link to Capt. John Jones's line

Evidence: David Gibbs owed rent to William R. Jones, who sent Sheriff McDonald with a casa (capias) against Gibbs. Jones agreed to wait until fall if Gibbs would pay in corn at the market price, and the sheriff was told to return the casa as “settled.” When the corn was ready, Jones would allow no more than nine shillings per barrel; Gibbs would not take that price but would take whatever Mr. Wm Porter would give. Henry Trucks was party to the arrangement (Thomas Gibbs affidavit, p.17: “Trux and said Jones agreed to take corn at the Market price in the fall if said Gibbs would pay him there”). The underlying suit at law (William R. Jones v Henry Trucks) went to five referees (bill, pp.3–4; Jones's answer, p.6). The arbitrators — Capt. Jas C. Steptoe, Thomas Lumpkin, William Cook (named by Burwell Gibbs, p.11) — met in the Clerk's office on a Saturday, both parties with witnesses, examined until near night, deferred, then met again the following Thursday (mail day) and made an award for the plaintiff of fifty dollars, returned and made a judgment of the court. Trucks's bill for injunction (Bedford July Court 1811, “presented” June 24, 1811 per endorsement p.2): he had no notice of the second meeting and never heard it; prays the judgment be enjoined. Jones's answer (filed July 8, year Unresolved — endorsement “Filed July 8th,” p.5): denies combination and fraud; says Trucks was present when the Thursday adjournment was agreed in the Clerk's office. Injunction bond (p.26): Henry Trucks & William Thomas, £30 Virginia money, to William R. Jones, dated January 7, 1814, signed with seals. Six affidavits taken January–February 1814: Jas C. Steptoe (pp.7–8; sworn June 25, 1814 before Charles Markley, JP); Burwell Gibbs (pp.11–12; sworn Feb 4, 1814 at the house of Armistead Otey, Liberty, before James Otey, JP, both parties present); Thomas Lumpkin (p.13; sworn Jan 29, 1814 before Charles Markley, JP); William Cook (p.15; sworn Jan 29, 1814 before Charles Markley, JP); Thomas Gibbs, son of David (pp.17–18; sworn Feb 7, 1814 before James Otey, JP); David Gibbs (pp.21–22; sworn Feb 17, 1814 before James Otey, JP). Document Title: 1837-016 (Lowry v. Perkins) — full 52-page firsthand read: the 12-acre title defect at Otter Mills (builds on DB1 519)
Document Type: Database entry — chancery manuscript firsthand read, complete file
Source: LVA, Bedford County Chancery Causes, 1837-016, William Lowry Jr. v. Abel B. Nichols, Simon M. Nock, John R. Perkins & Abraham/Abram Perkins (Elisha Perkins's heirs added by amended bill, May 1834); all 52 pages read visually 2026-09-23 (200-dpi grayscale; pp. 12, 41 re-rendered at 250–300 dpi)
Evidence: In 1828 William Lowry Jr. of Bedford bought 190 acres on the south side of the North Fork of Otter River from John R. & Abram Perkins of Fluvanna at $5/acre ($950 — computed from 190 × $5; the bill's sum is torn). He gave three purchase-money bonds, witnessed by Simon M. Nock and John Johnson. The Perkinses assigned the bonds: first to Simon M. Nock, then to Abel B. Nichols. Nichols took a law-side judgment (May 1833) against William Lowry Jr. and Milton Lowry; $170 of it was enjoined when Lowry filed his bill. Lowry's ground: the Perkinses had no title to 12 of the acres — the residue of an old parol exchange between Elisha Perkins (d. before the suit) and David Jones Sr. Abram's answer (sworn Mar 24, 1834, Amherst): Elisha conveyed Otter Mills and the surrounding land to John R. & Abram by deed 20 Feb 1819 (recorded Bedford 10 Apr 1819, p. 571) for $5,000 — but Elisha did not get the confirmatory 12-acre deed from David Jones until 17 Jul 1819 ($50; recorded p. 615), five months later. Plaintiff's counsel (Jno. F. Sale) argued the legal title was therefore outstanding in Elisha's heirs; defense (C. Dabney) answered that the warranty and after-acquired title perfected it. The bill was amended May 1834 to add Elisha's heirs. Nichols received $90 from Lowry on the judgment, 4 Jul 1835. The file ends with counsel's argument notes (Oct 1834); NO FINAL DECREE — outcome Unresolved. NO ENSLAVED PERSON appears anywhere in the 52 pages — bonds, deeds, depositions, and receipts concern only land, mill property, wheat, and money.
Why It Is Important: The direct legal sequel to 1836-032: Elisha, John R., Abram, William W. Perkins, Jno. Johnson, Simon M. Nock, and C. Dabney all appear in both files. David Jones Sr. — who in 1836-032 merely affirmed handwriting — here becomes a substantive deponent and adjoining landowner (deposed 8 May 1834 at his own dwelling house); his wife Martha Jones is named for the first time. The 1819 deed's $5,000 price and "late possessed... on Otter River" language corroborate the mill transaction history.
Connections: DB1 519 (the wealth-angle row); DB1 1539–1541 (1836-032); DB1 1543–1546 (deeds, heirs, Lowry); paper [414]

Document Title: The Drake verdicts: parceling for SALE not gift; abolitionism NOT supported; the Owen 'philanthropist' contamination
Document Type: Analytic verdicts on tested claims (secondary analysis of primary-adjacent evidence)
Source: Well-land-drake-report.md Target 4 (2026-09-23); H&D 2026 fns 73–74, 77, 81; UAH marker article; AHA 2020 transcript
Evidence: CLAIM (a) — PHILANTHROPY, TESTED, PARTLY SUPPORTED WITH A MAJOR CORRECTION. SUPPORTED: the Drakes did transfer former plantation land to formerly enslaved people — BY SALE, documented: Reuben Jones bought parcels from the Drakes in January 1871 (Deed Books TT p. 488; UU p. 350; DB1 rows 1521–1522). Drew Adan (AHA 2020 transcript): "they also portioned up smaller areas of the land and sold those off to descendants of the enslaved population that was at Avalon, including Shandy and Reuben Jones." UAH's marker article: "The Drakes facilitated parceling portions of the former plantation FOR SALE to the emancipated Jones slaves." An 1874 trustee sale of "Drake land" bounded "north by Wesley Jones's land" (DB1 row 1130) corroborates the parceling pattern in the deed record. THE CORRECTION: this was parceling for sale, NOT giving land back. No gift, donation, or below-market conveyance is documented. "Philanthropist" in the Drake network attaches most directly to ROBERT OWEN ("the Scotch philanthropist") — the Drakes' ASSOCIATE, not the Drakes themselves. Family-lore contamination risk identified: the "philanthropist" label may have migrated from Owen (via the New Harmony connection both Drakes held) onto the Drakes, then inflated "sold parcels to freedpeople" into "gave land back to freed slaves." The documented facts support: reformers who sold land to freedpeople. They do NOT support: philanthropists giving land back. CLAIM (b) — ABOLITIONISM, TESTED, NOT SUPPORTED. No documented anti-slavery activity by either Drake was found. What is documented is women's-SUFFRAGE activism (Priscilla, extensively; James as her political partner — "for many years, the women's suffrage movement in Alabama was represented only by Priscilla Holmes Drake and her husband"). Adjacent-but-not-equivalent facts that must not be blurred: Priscilla's friendship/correspondence with Lucretia Mott (a genuine abolitionist) and her parlor work with Robert Dale Owen (author of the abolitionist text The Wrong of Slavery, 1864) — on women's legal disabilities, NOT slavery. Association with abolitionists is not abolitionism. Counter-indicator: the Drakes moved to Alabama — a SLAVE STATE — IN 1861, at the outbreak of the Civil War. James P. Drake's party affiliation was DEMOCRATIC (antebellum Indiana Democrat, officeholder under Jackson/Monroe patronage networks) — the party of slavery's defense nationally in that era. Verdict: suffragists and social reformers — yes, solidly documented. Post-war land sales to freedpeople — yes, documented. Abolitionists — no evidence found; the label should not be used.

This protects the paper from the two most tempting overclaims in the Drake network and names the exact contamination pathway (Owen → Drakes) so the label migration doesn't creep back in. UAH's 2020s publications present the Drakes as "wellknown social reformers and women suffragists" (Adan) — the institution's current narrative leans on the reformer framing, which this verdict confirms while fencing the inflation.

Document Title: The Jones School, 1869–1870: the Bureau reports name it, and the rent shifted from Reuben to Crawford in January 1870
Document Type: Primary-source-anchored scholarship (H&D 2026, citing Freedmen's Bureau Teacher's Monthly School Reports)
Source: Hoksbergen & DeNeefe 2026, Alabama Review 79(3), pp. 216–217, fns 78–82; Freedmen's Bureau, Teacher's Monthly School Reports, March 1869–March 1870 (cited copies on file at Environmental Management Division, Dept. of Public Works, Garrison–Redstone Arsenal, Huntsville, AL); 1870 U.S. Federal Census, Madison County, AL, NARA M593, p. 13
Evidence: The March 1869–March 1870 school is documented in the PRIMARY record, not family lore: the Freedmen's Bureau Teacher's Monthly School Reports show Councill teaching the "JONES SCHOOL" and paying rent first to Reuben Jones, then — from JANUARY 1870 — to Thomas B. Crawford. Average attendance: ~39 students. REFINEMENT (changes the established framing): the rent paid TO REUBEN ran March–December 1869 only. From January 1870, rent shifted to Thomas B. Crawford, who had bought the surrounding 138 acres from the Drakes in January 1870 (H&D fn 81). So the "March 1869–March 1870 lease by Reuben" is slightly off: Reuben collected the rent for the first ten months; the school's last three months sat on Crawford-owned ground. This sharpens the thread; it does not contradict it. The lease was a MONTHLY RENTAL OF SPACE, not a recorded deed: no recorded lease instrument in the Madison County deed books has been located or cited anywhere; the evidence is the monthly rent line in the Bureau teacher reports. The Bureau reports themselves are not publicly viewable online in this pass — the cited copies sit at a military-installation office (Redstone Arsenal), not a public archive; free public routes are the NMAAHC Freedmen's Bureau Search Portal and FamilySearch's M810 index (whether the Madison County 1869–70 teacher reports are among the transcribed/indexed pages is Unresolved). Corroboration: the 1870 census (p. 13) places Councill, wife Elizabeth, and infant son William living next door to Reuben and Jane Jones, their two daughters, and Columbus's nineteen-year-old daughter Elizabeth, on the former plantation in Township 4, Range 1 West. School-name note: the Bureau record calls it the "Jones School"; the standard biographies' "Lincoln School, four miles west of Huntsville, in 1868" is very likely the same school under its community name (row 219's Adkins email already logs "Township 3 R 1 West," Lincoln School, and "Jones Place" as name variants) — but the Bureau's March 1869 start date is primary and should be preferred over the secondary 1868. THE PRE-1871 TITLE PUZZLE (evidenced skeleton, still unresolved): Reuben collected monthly school rent March–December 1869 on land he did not own in fee — he bought his Drake parcels in January 1871 (DB1 rows 1521–1522). The Bureau's rent ledger is the title-following evidence: rent to Reuben (Mar–Dec 1869) → rent to Crawford (from Jan 1870), because Crawford bought the surrounding 138 acres from the Drakes in January 1870. The rent followed the fee title — which means the school site lay inside Crawford's 138-acre purchase. Best-supported reading: Reuben, as a formerly-enslaved resident of the former Jones plantation, held the possessory interest (occupant/tenant) and sublet school space; the Bureau paid him as the person in possession. Consistent with his informal claims elsewhere: Reuben asserted "an additional sixty-seven acres just south of Athens Pike in the Northwest Quarter of Section 4, T4S-R1W, although his claim was never formalized with a deed" — in 1874 that parcel was put up for public auction for unpaid taxes assessed to "Reuben Jones and others" (Huntsville Weekly Democrat, Feb 12, 1874; H&D fn 77).
Why It Is Important: This anchors the project's most important institutional thread — Reuben Jones → Councill's 1869 school → the institution that became Alabama A&M — to the primary Bureau record via published scholarship, and it corrects the lease framing in two precise ways: the "Jones School" name and the January 1870 rent shift. The rent-shift is also the cleanest title-chain evidence in the whole 1869–70 puzzle: rent follows fee title. The paper's Jones School section can now be anchored to the Bureau reports via H&D 2026 rather than resting on the project notes alone.
